items.title: Announcing New vLLM and SGLang Inference Engines on TPU
items.summary: This post announces native PyTorch backends for vLLM and SGLang powered by TorchTPU, enabling developers to run and optimize serving workloads using familiar PyTorch tools. Public benchmarks demonstrate state-of-the-art performance and industry-leading cost efficiency on Ironwood TPU across long-context and agentic workloads.

items.title: Agent Distraction
items.summary: Analysis of over 913,000 coding agent sessions reveals that 13% expose agents to inline TODO(b/...) comments. In 6% of encounters, agents act on these comments, with 83% being entirely unprompted by the developer. These detours result in significant overhead—adding 70% more steps, 77% more tokens, and 105% more wait time per session—split between chasing closed tickets (41%) and unauthorized scope creep on open bugs (57%). Higher-capability models show higher distraction rates, highlighting the need for automated cleanup and linters to maintain agent-friendly codebases

items.title: What is Pathways? Single-controller training for large models
items.summary: Pathways is a single-controller distributed training system designed to coordinate large-scale model training across multiple accelerator groups by representing computations as a global dataflow graph. Unlike traditional SPMD models like DDP and FSDP that rely on synchronous collectives, Pathways uses asynchronous dispatch and a central scheduler to maximize hardware utilization and prevent deadlocks in complex workloads. By decoupling model definition from physical hardware via virtual devices, developers can efficiently scale complex training architectures and seamlessly handle dynamic workloads like reinforcement learning post-training.

items.title: Nodejs Daily Email Sending with Third-Party Scheduling and Idempotent Retries
items.summary: For a daily support report or a renewal reminder, use a scheduling service to trigger a small public HTTP handler and let an email provider deliver the message. Keep the business deadline in the payload, and make the handler idempotent before you add retries. That split leaves scheduling, retry delivery, and email deliverability outside the application process without turning the deadline rule into an invisible cron job. The important design choice is not “which cron syntax?” It is what happens when the scheduler retries after a timeout. A reminder must not be sent twice because the first request reached the email provider and the response disappeared. Store a delivery key such as accountId:deadlineDate, claim it atomically, and only then send. If the send operation itself can be retried, use the same key at that boundary too. For teams already assembling backend services, Infrai is a plausible middle layer for this job: its scheduling and queue capabilities sit behind one REST contract and one key. items.title: CSV to JSON Converter: When One Quoted Comma Broke 4,112 Supplier Records
items.summary: CSV to JSON Converter: When One Quoted Comma Broke 4,112 Supplier Records Every quarter I pull two supplier price lists into our internal pricing API. Supplier A exports comma-separated CSV from an old Windows ERP. Supplier B sends semicolon-separated files with German decimal commas and a byte-order mark nobody warned me about. The API only speaks JSON. For three quarters my sync script was fourteen lines of Node. It worked, which is the worst thing a parser can do. Then supplier A shipped the full catalog instead of the usual 400-row delta, and 4,112 of 12,417 rows landed with the wrong number of fields. The API accepted them all, because nothing in JSON complains when amount becomes a string holding half a company name. This is the version of that script I run now, plus two other routes I keep around when I'm debugging at 11 pm. The csv module has shipped with Python since 2.3 and handles RFC 4180 quoting, but only once you tell it which delimiter you have and refuse to continue when a row doesn't line up. items.title: Debugging Electron Apps: A Practical Guide to Main, Renderer, and Production
items.summary: Every Electron developer has lived this moment: the app works in dev, then ships to a user and misbehaves in a way you cannot reproduce. Stack Overflow answers fragment the debugging story across a dozen flags and launch args, and half of them are stale. This is the field guide I wish I'd had at version 1.0 — one reference for the main process, the renderer, utility processes, packaged builds, and the small set of tricks that turn "it works on my machine" into a reproducible bug. Main process: launch with --inspect=5858 and attach VS Code or Chrome DevTools to about:inspect. Breakpoints in main.ts work the same way as in Node. Renderer: mainWindow.webContents.openDevTools({ mode: 'detach' }) — but gate it behind an env var or a hidden menu item so it never ships to users. Packaged app: re-run the installed binary from a terminal with --enable-logging --remote-debugging-port=9222; console.log from main and renderer will both land in stdout, and Chrome on localhost:9222 gets you full DevTools. Production debugging: don't attach to a stranger's machine. Ship a "Diagnostics" modal that captures a crash dump, a recent log tail, and the GPU process info, and send it to your crash endpoin

items.summary: Short answer: use staged retrieval for a legal contract review workspace, with an explicit collection, a bounded query at every stage, preserved tenant and access metadata, and a source identifier on every returned passage; trigger a fallback only for a named failure condition, then record which stage produced the answer. The decision is operational, not cosmetic. A fallback that silently broadens a query may raise recall while crossing an access boundary or burying the clause a reviewer needed. Start with representative contracts and known failure cases, measure recall and precision, and make each recovery step visible in traces. items.title: Day 17: The Connector and the Convergence of Client Responsibilities
items.summary: The previous post, JSON-RPC 2.0: Protocol Choice and the Request Pipeline, was about how a call is handled once it reaches the server. The same contract needs somebody responsible on the client side too: some clients connect to a server on the other side of a network, and some run in the same process as the back end logic, yet both are calling the same method. If everything in between that has nothing to do with the business is left to each front end, there will be as many ways of writing it as there are front ends, and the same mistake will happen once in every one of them. The framework's answer is a Connector layer on the client side as well, which every front end goes through. This post covers: Which things the client has to handle, and why they are collected into one type How a local and a remote connection become the same call, and where the real difference lies Which state belongs to one logged in user, and which belongs to the whole application The layers one save passes through, from the screen to the database, are fixed: Client screen ↓ DataObject: the framework's ViewModel, wrapping a DataSet for the screen to bind to ↓ Connector (this post) ↓ one JSON-RPC call Server AP

The browser already had plenty of JavaScript. Yet the next screen still waited for a network round trip. The missing piece was the React Server Component payload for the destination route. Data may still be loading, but the application can show its own loading UI immediately. Server Components change what the browser has available. Their implementation stays on the server. items.title: Rate-Limited Job Processing: Cron or Queue for a Node.js Backend
items.summary: For rate-limited job processing, choose cron or a queue based on recovery state, then enforce the per-minute limit where a Node.js backend makes the downstream call. The useful choice is the smallest system that can replay interrupted work without repeating an external effect. Short answer: use a scheduled scan for bounded, reconcilable work; add durable per-item state when jobs need independent pacing, retries, and an audit trail. I treat this as an experiment, not a throughput contest. A simple scheduled process can look perfect in a notebook, then hide the hard question: what records that item 1,137 completed when the process stops between the downstream call and its own state update? If the answer is "the next run will find it," that can be a sound design. If the answer depends on remembering each delivery, the state has to be explicit. Put the rate limit immediately before the downstream request. A producer-side limit only controls admission; retries, another producer, or a restarted worker can still create a burst at the API boundary. One worker can keep timestamps locally. items.title: React Email Verification States That Explain Themselves
items.summary: Email verification looks like a small form until you ship it. Then the edge cases arrive: the request is still running, the code is wrong, the link expired, the user clicked resend twice, or the browser came back from a suspended tab. Many React forms start with three booleans: const [loading, setLoading] = useState(false); const [error, setError] = useState (null); const [verified, setVerified] = useState(false); This is friendly at first, but it can describe impossible combinations. What does loading: true and verified: true mean? Should an old error remain visible while a new request is running? Can the resend button be enabled during a code submission? The important part are the transitions, not the number of variables. A verification flow should tell the user what is happening and what action is safe next. items.title: The Page Looks Ready. Your Browser Test Disagrees.
items.summary: A user opens a page, sees a button, and clicks it. Your automated test opens the same page, sees the same button, and fails. Sometimes the button is replaced a moment later. Sometimes a loading skeleton looks enough like the real component to confuse a selector. Sometimes the browser's address bar changes the available space, and an element moves just as the test tries to click it. The application might be broken. The test might be broken. Or both might be behaving exactly as designed, just at different moments. That's what makes modern browser testing frustrating. We build increasingly dynamic interfaces, then write tests as if pages appear all at once and stay put. Consider an app using React Suspense and server-side rendering. The server sends HTML. The browser displays it. A person looking at the screen thinks the page is ready. But JavaScript may still be loading, data may still be resolving, and React may still be attaching event handlers or replacing parts of the DOM. Your test finds the Save button and clicks it. Nothing happens. So someone adds a two-second wait. That seems to fix it, until CI gets a little slower. The better approach is to test readiness, not elapsed time

items.title: Your .Net Blazor Skills Just Became Blockchain Skills
items.summary: I've been writing C# for years. Enterprise systems, CRMs, the kind of code that runs quietly in the background and pays the bills. When I started getting curious about blockchain, I assumed I'd have to leave all of that behind and start over in JavaScript, Rust, or Solidity. It turns out I didn't. On the Internet Computer (ICP), a whole web app, frontend included, can be served straight from the blockchain. And Blazor WebAssembly compiles to exactly the kind of static files ICP's asset canisters know how to serve. So I tried it. It worked in the end, but the road there was full of potholes nobody had documented. This article is the map I wish I'd had, plus a template that lets you skip straight to the fun part. If you open the ICP tooling today and look for a template, you'll find options for React, Svelte, Vue, and plain JavaScript. For C# developers, there was nothing. So I built one. As far as I can find, this is the first Blazor template for icp-cli: one command gives you a Blazor WebAssembly frontend and a Motoko backend, deployed together on the Internet Computer. To be fair, I'm not the first person to run Blazor on ICP. Michiel Post's Dfinity.Blazor library and the ICP.NET

items.title: Why Disabling the Submit Button Isn't Enough: Preventing Duplicate Requests in React & Node.js
items.summary: Imagine this scenario: A customer clicks Place Order. The request reaches your server, the database successfully creates the order, but the response never reaches the browser because of a network issue. The customer assumes something went wrong and clicks again. Now you have two orders instead of one. This is a common reliability problem in web applications. Disabling a submit button might prevent accidental double-clicks, but it doesn't guarantee that an operation will execute only once. Let's explore how to handle this properly using React, Node.js, and PostgreSQL. In React, we often prevent repeated submissions using a loading state: const [isSubmitting, setIsSubmitting] = useState(false); async function handleSubmit() { if (isSubmitting) return; setIsSubmitting(true); try { await createOrder(); } finally { setIsSubmitting(false); } } This is useful for improving the user experience. But there is a problem. Duplicate requests can still happen because of: Network retries Multiple browser tabs Concurrent API calls Repeated webhook deliveries Client or server failures Even rapid calls within the same render cycle can observe the same React state before an update takes effect. items.title: Your users upload 12MP phone photos. Your app shouldn't serve them raw.
items.summary: If you have ever wired up an ASP.NET Core photo upload and watched a 12-megapixel phone JPEG land in blob storage at full size, sideways, with GPS still in the EXIF, you already know the feeling. The endpoint works. The CDN bill and the broken avatars arrive later. I also know the other path by heart: pull in SkiaSharp, remember which native asset package Linux needs, apply EXIF orientation yourself, pick a fit mode that does not letterbox by accident, binary-search JPEG quality until the file is under 100 KB, and hope nobody posts a decompression bomb. It works. It is also easy to get slightly wrong on the second feature. So I built PicReady: a small .NET 8/9 library that wraps SkiaSharp for the everyday web-app jobs — resize, crop, avatar, WebP, strip EXIF, hit a max byte size — behind a short fluent API. PicReady.Lite is the free MIT subset for a plain resize. This post is the problem, the API, real numbers from one stopwatch run, and when you should not use it. Phone cameras send large JPEGs. items.title: Why am I building one more UI component lib in AI age?
items.summary: We've never had so much power to build software. You can turn an idea into a working app in a day/hour/minute? But there's always a catch: You AI agent can solve it too. So the question is: does anyone actually need what we/you/me're building? I've been working in product development, open source, and startups for years, and this question has never felt more closer to home. Every day we see more and more apps, but it's not always clear who the end user is or what problem it's going solving. We've been working on our data grid library, RevoGrid, for quite a few years now (closer to decade if we count for Open Source part). It's an Excel-like data grid you can put into your app. Over this time, we've built so many components and tried so many approaches that you could probably build an entire Power BI on top of it. We've spent even more time testing it and solving quests of "what to do next?" So recently, we spent a week of our lives extracting these components into a separate UI library and making it available to everyone. What's inside? items.title: I published the beta of my bubble chart library. Help me break it!
items.summary: In January I posted a crypto bubble chart I'd built from scratch on Threads. Few people saw it. Ten months, one redesign and a lot of tests later, it's a library: OrbFlow. It's a bubble chart for the web where the bubbles act like bubbles. They rise in when the chart scrolls into view, float, push each other apart, and pop when you tap one. Today the beta is on npm, and I'd like you to try to break it. npm i orbflow@beta React (18 or 19, works with Next.js): import { OrbChart } from "orbflow/react"; export default function App() { return ( console.log(orb.label)} /> ); } Plain JavaScript: import { OrbChart } from "orbflow"; const chart = new OrbChart("#chart"); chart.setData([ { id: "a", label: "Apples", value: 40 }, { id: "b", label: "Pears", value: 25 }, ]); Give the container a size and the chart fills it. items.title: Downloaded Is Not Selected: Managing Whisper and Qwen Models in a Native Voice App
items.summary: An “offline AI” switch hides several different questions: is a model present, are its companion files present, and is the runtime actually using it? Treating those as one boolean produces confusing settings and difficult support reports. The local-model catalog in GPT Realtime Assistant makes those distinctions explicit. This article focuses on the inspected download service rather than making a latency claim about every device or language. RealtimeDownloadableModel entries identify a repository, a remote filename, a destination filename, and an installation kind. The catalog includes Whisper Large v3 Turbo variants and Qwen 3 8B variants with different quantizations. That metadata is operational configuration. “Qwen” is not enough information to select a compatible file or explain its storage cost. The precise artifact matters, and companion artifacts can matter too. The status builder resolves the runtime’s chosen Whisper, Qwen, and Qwen-ASR paths separately. For each catalog entry it inspects the local file size and checks that required companion files exist. It reports isInstalled separately from isSelected. items.summary: Epic Games says it plans to support its new Linux launcher on as many distributions as possible, specifically naming Fedora, SteamOS, CachyOS and Omarchy. GamingOnLinux's Liam Squires-Hand reports: Speaking to Jake Jones, Communications Director at Epic Games, they said: "Hey Liam! The new Epic Games Launcher is still in Preview and we plan to support as many Linux distributions as possible, including Fedora, SteamOS, Cachy, Omarchy, and more. We're testing and evaluating packaging formats for distribution, and we'll restore AppImage this month." With that in mind, until things settle down, you might see different packaging types appear or disappear until they decide firmly how they plan to support different distributions each with their own different packaging formats. Or, perhaps they might see the Flatpak light and just put it up officially on Flathub. items.title: How Does BreathTime’s Petition System Actually Work?
items.summary: How Does BreathTime’s Petition System Actually Work? BreathTime is a small civic platform: people propose petitions, sign them, and leave a few words of support. This post walks through exactly how each of those steps works today — including the parts that are deliberately simple, and the parts that don't exist yet. Any registered, logged-in user can suggest a petition through the Propose a Petition page. A proposal has three fields: a title a description of what should change and why an addressee — the government, institution or organisation the petition is aimed at The form is a React page that sends the proposal to an API route; the server checks that the user is signed in (NextAuth) and saves it to the database (Prisma + MySQL) with the status pending. Every proposal is read by a person. In the admin panel, proposals are listed newest first, with the author's name. For each one, the administrator can: approve it, or reject it, optionally adding a comment. Either way, the author gets an in-app notification — and on a rejection, the admin's comment is included so they know why. items.title: Modern SFTP in .NET 8: Resilience, Dependency Injection, and Zero-Disk Streams
items.summary: In the era of microservices, event streaming, and cloud-native architectures, many developers are surprised to discover that mission-critical enterprise workflows still run on... SFTP. From banking reconciliation files (ACH/SEPA/CNAB) and healthcare records (HL7/EDI) to ERP batch processing (SAP/Oracle), SFTP remains the de facto protocol for secure, asynchronous B2B data exchange. However, a quick search for C# SFTP tutorials reveals an unfortunate reality: most guides still promote patterns from a decade ago. They use synchronous blocking I/O, tightly couple business logic to concrete client classes, rely on temporary disk files, and lack automatic reconnects or transient fault handling. items.title: SaveChanges shouldn't take four seconds to insert 100,000 rows
items.summary: If you have ever watched an import job stall after AddRange and SaveChanges, you already know the feeling. EF Core is doing honest work: it tracks every entity, generates commands, and talks to SQL Server more than you wanted. That is the right tradeoff when you are saving a cart or a user profile. It is a painful one when you are writing thousands or hundreds of thousands of rows. I also know the other path by heart: SqlBulkCopy into a temp table, a MERGE with HOLDLOCK so two imports do not race, a transaction you actually commit, and a decision about identity values. It works. It is also easy to get slightly wrong. So I built SqlBulkPro: a small .NET 8/9 library that uses SqlBulkCopy and MERGE under the hood and gives you one method for the usual cases. It works with EF Core and with Dapper / ADO.NET. This post is the problem, the API, real numbers from one benchmark machine, and when you should not use it. SaveChanges slows down at volume EF Core is a change tracker first and a SQL generator second. For a handful of rows that is a gift. items.title: Microsoft.Testing.Platform: How .NET Testing Evolved
items.summary: For most .NET developers, running tests has long appeared simple: add MSTest, NUnit, or xUnit.net, write a few test methods, and run dotnet test. Under that command, however, sits a test platform responsible for discovering tests, loading adapters, starting processes, collecting results, and integrating with editors and CI systems. That distinction matters: A test framework defines how tests are written. Examples include MSTest, NUnit, xUnit.net, and TUnit. A test platform discovers and executes those tests and connects them to command-line tools, IDEs, and build pipelines. For many years, VSTest was the standard platform behind .NET testing. Microsoft.Testing.Platform (MTP) is its modern, lightweight alternative. It does not replace test frameworks; instead, it changes how their tests are hosted and executed. The earliest .NET test runners were closely associated with their frameworks or development environments. Tests often ran through a framework-specific console runner or directly inside Visual Studio. items.summary: Anthropic has released Claude Mythos 5.2 and Fable 5.2 with "improvements in areas like coding, reasoning, and vision," while cutting Fable's input price and claiming 30% faster responses. TechCrunch reports: It's Anthropic's first model release since the arrival of a third-party report from the assessment group METR, which suggested the lab might be approaching recursive self-improvement (RSI) -- or the ability for AI models to carry on model training independently. The METR report found internal models were speeding up Anthropic's AI progress by roughly 2x, although many uncertainties remain. Still, Anthropic's release notes significant ongoing challenges in accurately testing model capabilities. "Claude Mythos 5.2 and Fable 5.2 each voice suspicion that they are being evaluated more often than any of our recent models, which challenges our ability to assess how they will act in real-world settings. Learning the fundamentals is important, but professional developers also need to understand modern development tools, architectural approaches, and emerging best practices. items.title: Exploring ReactJS Testing Techniques for Better Code Quality
items.summary: Writing functional code is only one part of successful application development. Developers must also ensure that their applications behave correctly under different conditions. Testing plays an important role in identifying errors, preventing unexpected behaviour, and maintaining application quality. ReactJS developers can use several testing techniques to verify individual components, user interactions, and complete application workflows. Understand the Importance of Component Testing React applications are built using reusable components. A component may display information, accept user input, or perform specific actions when users interact with it. Component testing helps developers verify whether individual components behave as expected. For example, a login button should respond correctly when clicked, while an input field should accept and display the entered value. Testing components independently makes it easier to identify problems before they affect the entire application. Use Jest for JavaScript Testing Jest is a widely used JavaScript testing framework. The move broadens Google's challenge to Nvidia as demand outstrips supply, with Google saying every TPU it currently has is already committed to customers. Quartz reports: The 8tx is designed for sensitive, privacy-focused jobs run by clients including public-sector bodies and businesses in heavily regulated sectors, according to Bloomberg. It pairs with a central processing unit from Advanced Micro Devices and encrypts data at the chip level. Normally, data must be decrypted in memory as the machine works on it, [said Amin Vahdat, Chief Technologist for AI & Infrastructure at Google]. The 8i Max is meant for AI applications that need long context windows, meaning the volume of information a model can take into account within one request. items.title: I turned C# compiler errors into a game of Snake
items.summary: Every C# editor has a tiny graphics card hiding in it. It only draws three colours, it only refreshes when you type, and most people spend their whole day trying to make it go blank. It's the error squiggle. I built Snake on it. Squiggly is a NuGet package. Add it to a project, create a file with // squiggly on the first line, press Ctrl+. and pick New game: Snake. The snake's head is a red error. Its body is a row of yellow warnings. The food is those faint grey dots you've been ignoring for years. It works in Visual Studio, VS Code (with C# Dev Kit) and Rider, and there's no plugin for any of them. It's just an analyzer. There's Tetris and Minesweeper too, because once you have a screen, you kind of have to. If you've never written one: Roslyn, the C# compiler, lets you plug in your own checks. An analyzer is a class that gets handed your code and can report diagnostics. Those are the same kind of thing as CS0103: The name 'x' does not exist, and your editor draws them as squiggles. The severity picks the colour: errors are red, warnings are yellow (green in Visual Studio), and info shows up as a few grey dots. The other half is code fixes, which is the lightbulb menu. items.title: Authentication and Authorization: What's New in .NET 11
items.summary: When it comes to authentication and authorization, .NET 11 focuses on valuable refinements. It addresses key edge cases to enhance security and user experience: a WebSocket that outlives its access token, an authorization attribute that works on one endpoint type but not on another, a passkey list full of identical "Passkey" labels. Let's look at what the newest release brings to authentication and authorization. A SignalR connection can live for hours, while an access token usually doesn't. Until now, you had two unattractive options when the token expired: close the connection and make the client reconnect (missing messages in the gap), or leave it open and keep trusting an identity that is no longer valid. .NET 11 adds a third option: authentication refresh. The client sends the old token over a dedicated /refresh endpoint, and the server swaps the connection's ClaimsPrincipal in place. items.title: .NET 8 and 9 lose support on Nov 10. Your image tags won't tell you which pods run them.
items.summary: Tomorrow, November 10, 2026, .NET 8 and .NET 9 both reach end of support. .NET 8 was the LTS release and .NET 9 the STS one, and they end on the same day. After that, neither gets security patches. .NET 10 is the LTS to move to, supported until November 14, 2028. If you run .NET on Kubernetes, the first question is a boring one, and it's harder than it sounds: which of the containers running right now are actually on 8 or 9? I spent some time on this while building runtime checks for Runtimez, and the image tag turned out to be the least useful place to look. mcr.microsoft.com/dotnet/aspnet:8.0 is easy. The version is right there. But almost nobody runs that image directly. You build your own: FROM mcr.microsoft.com/dotnet/aspnet:8.0 COPY publish/ /app ENTRYPOINT ["dotnet", "/app/Orders.Api.dll"] and push it as registry.example.com/orders-api:1.42. Now the tag is your app's version, and the .NET version is gone from everything kubectl get pods shows you. The usual next move is kubectl exec and dotnet --list-runtimes. That works until you hit a chiseled image, which has no shell. It also means exec-ing into production pods to answer an inventory question, which I'd rather avoid. Mic

We explore how its cultural references, rebel spirit and sprawling sense of freedom make it a definitive work of art In the 00s, when the Grand Theft Auto developer Rockstar Games revealed a new project, video game writers from all over the UK would make the journey to the company’s office in London. They would be ushered one by one into a darkened room to sit facing an enormous TV. There would be a dish of sweets on a low bench in front of them but, in the reverential hush that descended, it was never entirely clear if it was acceptable to eat them. After a few moments, the screen would come to life. Rockstar would sometimes begin its presentation not with footage from its new game, but clips from classic movies. This is the context of what we are making, Rockstar was saying, and that is where we belong. Continue reading...

items.title: iOS Silent Push Notifications That Actually Arrive: content-available, Priority 5 and the Throttling Rules
items.summary: Silent push notifications (Apple calls them background notifications) are the push you send when you don't want to show anything. You just want the app to wake up, fetch new data, refresh a cache or sync a record. They're also the push type developers most often swear "doesn't work." Usually it does work. It just follows rules that visible alerts don't. This guide covers the exact payload and headers, the app-side code, and the reasons a silent push gets delayed or dropped. A silent push is a payload with content-available set to 1 and no alert, sound or badge: { "aps": { "content-available": 1 }, "type": "sync", "since": "2026-11-09T04:00:00Z" } Anything outside aps is your own data and is handed to the app. Keep the total under 4 KB. If you add an alert to the same payload, it's no longer a silent push. It becomes a visible notification that also happens to wake the app, and it follows the visible-alert rules instead. When you call APNs over HTTP/2, a background notification needs these headers: Header Value apns-push-type background apns-priority 5 apns-topic your app's bundle ID Two rules matter here: apns-push-type must be background. items.title: A Mute Button Must Fail Closed: Recording App and Microphone Audio with ReplayKit
items.summary: A screen recording can look correct while sounding completely wrong. A tutorial needs narration above the application’s audio; a demonstration may need only system sound. Treating both inputs as one volume control makes those two jobs unnecessarily difficult. In Reel Screen Recorder, the broadcast extension receives ReplayKit buffers and keeps their source identity until the writer dispatches them. The useful engineering detail is not the slider itself. It is what happens when transforming a buffer fails. The current SampleHandler.handleAudio distinguishes .audioMic from .audioApp and asks the shared settings for recordingGain(forMicrophone:). It then passes the processed buffer, with its original source type, to BroadcastWriter. The writer routes video, app audio, and microphone audio to separate capture functions. Its asset writer uses the MP4 container. This division keeps capture policy out of the file-writing dispatch code and makes it possible to reason about each source independently. items.title: Breathe as One: a two-phone co-op game you win by breathing together
items.summary: This is a submission for the Presage SmartSpectra SDK Challenge Breathe as One is a little co-op game for two people and two iPhones. You win by breathing together. You sit across from each other with your phones propped up, front cameras facing you. Each phone only watches its own player. The SmartSpectra SDK picks up the rise and fall of your chest and turns it into a live wave, and the two phones swap those waves over a private nearby connection. So both screens show the same thing: your breath in blue and your partner's in coral. As you settle into the same rhythm, the two lines drift toward each other's color until they melt into one lilac line. Getting there is the whole game. A game takes a few minutes and has three rounds: Follow the Tide (45 s). A white wave rolls across the screen at 6 breaths a minute, and you both ride it. No Leader (60 s). The wave goes away and you have to find each other without a guide. It's harder than it sounds, and it's my favorite part. Heart Meet (45 s). As the year has passed, however, what once seemed like a new industrial juggernaut has ground to a halt. items.title: ‘There is no inevitable dystopia’: Jeanette Winterson on AI and the future of humanity
items.summary: The author believes we are at a turning point as a species – and even in the shadow of big tech it’s up to us how we want to proceed ‘I am a storyteller by trade,” writes Jeanette Winterson on the first page of her 2021 book 12 Bytes, an idiosyncratic and thought-provoking series of essays in which she considered just how artificial intelligence might change everything about our lives. “And I know everything we do is a fiction until it’s a fact: the dream of flying, the dream of space travel, the dream of speaking to someone instantly, across time and space, the dream of not dying – or of returning.” She had already been thinking about our possible futures for at least 15 years – her 2007 novel, The Stone Gods, for instance, imagined a post-climate catastrophe world populated by robots and humans who never age, while 12 Bytes was preceded by Frankisstein: A Love Story, which alternates a recreation of the summer Mary Shelley wrote Frankenstein with a trans doctor’s travels among present-day cryogenecists and AI-enabled robots.
